## What it is

Good scientists get *upset* by anomalies: a data point that shouldn't be there, a result that contradicts the model, a number that doesn't add up. They don't explain it away as noise or move on. They take the discomfort as a signal that their understanding is incomplete, and they track down the cause. That capacity to be bothered is what turns surprises into discoveries.

## Why it matters

Most anomalies are noise, so there's a temptation to ignore all of them. But some aren't, and those are where new understanding comes from: a data error, a broken model, a new phenomenon. A researcher who is never upset never finds them. One who is upset by everything never finishes. The skill is calibrated upset-ness: noticing deviations bigger than the noise can explain, and following them up.

## How it works

Think of it as anomaly detection with a threshold. Flag a residual when it exceeds $k$ standard deviations of what the model expects. A high $k$ (hard to upset) misses real anomalies. A low $k$ (easily upset) chases noise. The researcher with a well-calibrated $k$, who also *investigates* what they flag, catches the real problems at a manageable cost in false alarms.

## Simulated example

A stream of 300 measurements fits a model well, except that a real anomaly, a shift caused by an undetected problem, starts partway through. Set how easily the researcher gets upset.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof k = Inputs.range([1, 5], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "How hard to upset (flag residuals beyond k sd)"})
viewof shift = Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 1.2, step: 0.1, label: "Size of the real anomaly (sd units)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 146, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
upset = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  return range(300).map(t => {
    const real = t >= 200 && t < 240;
    const resid = r.normal(real ? shift : 0, 1);
    return {t, resid, real, flagged: Math.abs(resid) > k};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 280,
  x: {label: "Measurement"},
  y: {label: "Residual from the model (sd units)", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rect([0], {x1: 200, x2: 240, y1: -5, y2: 6, fill: "#e6ab02", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.dot(upset, {x: "t", y: "resid", r: d => d.flagged ? 4 : 2, fill: d => d.flagged ? "#d6604d" : "#999"}),
    Plot.ruleY([k, -k], {stroke: "#d6604d", strokeDasharray: "4 3"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const hit = upset.filter(d => d.real && d.flagged).length, falseA = upset.filter(d => !d.real && d.flagged).length;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`The shaded zone is the real anomaly. The researcher flags **${hit}** of its 40 points, along with **${falseA}** false alarms elsewhere. ${hit === 0 ? "Never upset, so the problem goes unnoticed." : falseA > 30 ? "Upset by everything, so the real signal is buried in false alarms." : "Upset in the right places, so there's something worth tracking down."}`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Treat anomalies as information about what you don't understand.
- Calibrate how easily you get upset: not by every wiggle, and not by nothing.
- Follow up. Being upset is only useful if it leads to an investigation.
:::
